# Is an Egg a Day Bad for Your Heart? A Research Review

## Bottom line up front

For a **healthy adult, eating about one egg a day is not meaningfully bad for your heart.** The best-adjusted large studies find no significant association between roughly one egg per day and cardiovascular disease, and randomized feeding trials show that eating eggs within an otherwise sensible diet moves blood cholesterol very little. The evidence supports **up to one whole egg per day for healthy adults** as a safe default, consistent with the current American Heart Association and British Heart Foundation positions.

The important caveats — spelled out below — are that (1) the evidence is dominated by observational studies that cannot fully separate "eggs" from "the bacon, buttered toast, and lifestyle that often come with eggs" in Western diets; (2) a genuine, repeatedly observed signal suggests eggs are riskier for people **with type 2 diabetes**; and (3) what matters far more than the egg is the **rest of the plate** — eggs raise cholesterol far less than the saturated fat they are frequently cooked and served with.

---

## 1. Why this question is genuinely contested

Eggs are the most concentrated common source of dietary cholesterol (~185–200 mg in one large egg's yolk). For decades this earned them a hard cap (the old "no more than 300 mg cholesterol/day," i.e., under two eggs). The science that dismantled that cap is the reason the answer today is "mostly fine" rather than "avoid" — but the picture is not uniformly reassuring, and honest reporting requires showing where the studies disagree.

The disagreement is real and falls into three camps:

- **"No effect"** — the largest and best-adjusted cohorts and the biggest meta-analysis.
- **"Modest harm"** — one influential US pooled analysis, plus a consistent harm signal for heart failure and for people with diabetes.
- **"Modest benefit"** — large Asian cohorts.

These are not contradictions to be papered over; they are informative, and the pattern of who finds what is itself the key to the answer.

---

## 2. The prospective cohort studies (millions of people, observational)

### The "no effect" evidence (the mainstream finding)

The most rigorous analysis pools the three great US health-professional cohorts — the Nurses' Health Study I and II and the Health Professionals Follow-Up Study — 215,618 people followed up to 32 years, 14,806 cardiovascular events. Comparing **≥1 egg/day vs <1 egg/month**, the pooled hazard ratio for incident CVD was **0.93 (95% CI 0.82–1.05)** — no significant association. When the authors folded this into an updated meta-analysis of 1,720,108 participants, the pooled relative risk per **1 additional egg/day** was **0.98 (95% CI 0.93–1.03)** — essentially flat.
Source (verified): Drouin-Chartier et al., *BMJ* 2020;368:m513 — https://www.bmj.com/content/368/bmj.m513 · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32132002/

The international **PURE study** (146,011 people across 50 countries, ~9.5 years) agreed: comparing ≥7 eggs/week vs <1/week, the HR was **1.04 (0.94–1.15)** for total mortality and **0.92 (0.83–1.01)** for major CVD — no significant effect either way.
Source (verified): Dehghan et al., *Am J Clin Nutr* 2020 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7138651/

### The "harm" evidence (the notable outlier)

The single most-cited study pointing the other way pooled six US cohorts (29,615 adults, median 17.5 years). Each **additional half-egg per day** was associated with a higher risk:
- Incident CVD: **HR 1.06 (95% CI 1.03–1.10)**; absolute risk difference +1.11%
- All-cause mortality: **HR 1.08 (95% CI 1.04–1.11)**; absolute risk difference +1.93%

Source (verified directly from full text): Zhong et al., *JAMA* 2019 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6439941/

This is the strongest harm signal, and it is dose-responsive, which is why it made headlines. But two things temper it. First, diet was measured **once, at baseline** (a snapshot, sometimes decades before events). Second, and more importantly, the effect was tied to **total dietary cholesterol** (HR 1.17 per 300 mg/day) — the egg association weakened once the analysis accounted for overall cholesterol and red-meat intake, so it is hard to say the egg itself, rather than the total dietary-cholesterol-and-meat load it travels with, carried the risk.

### The "benefit" evidence (large, but Asian)

The **China Kadoorie Biobank** (461,213 adults, ~8.9 years) found daily egg eaters had *lower* risk than rare eaters:
- Total CVD: **HR 0.89 (0.87–0.92)**
- Ischemic heart disease: **0.88 (0.84–0.93)**
- Hemorrhagic stroke: **0.74 (0.67–0.82)**
- CVD death: **0.82 (0.75–0.89)**

Source (verified): Qin et al., *Heart* 2018 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6241631/

This benefit is almost certainly not because eggs protect the heart. In China, daily egg intake tends to mark a *better*, more affluent, more varied diet, whereas in the US eggs are eaten at low average intake and often alongside processed meat and refined carbohydrates. This East–West split is the single most important interpretive clue in the whole literature (see §3).

**What all cohort studies share as a weakness:** they are observational; diet is self-reported and usually captured once; and none can fully rule out that healthier or less-healthy *overall eating patterns* — not eggs — drive the numbers. This is why randomized trials matter.

---

## 3. Meta-analyses and the shape of the dose-response

Pooling dozens of cohorts, the per-egg association with **coronary heart disease and stroke is essentially null**:

- Rong et al., *BMJ* 2013 (up to ~7 million person-years): per 1 egg/day, CHD **RR 0.99 (0.85–1.15)** and stroke **RR 0.91 (0.81–1.02)**, both non-significant, with zero heterogeneity (I²=0%). — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3538567/
- Shin et al., *Am J Clin Nutr* 2013 (22 cohorts): overall CVD **HR 0.96 (0.88–1.05)**. — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23676423/
- Krittanawong et al., *Am J Med* 2021 (23 studies, ~1.4 million people): overall CVD **HR 0.99 (0.93–1.06)**; coronary artery disease actually **0.89 (0.86–0.93)**. — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32653422/
- Godos et al., *Eur J Nutr* 2021 (dose-response, ~2 million people): a shallow inverse association up to about **1 egg/day (CVD summary RR 0.94, 0.89–0.99)** that then plateaus; **stroke null**. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8137614/

Two consistent, credible signals emerge from the meta-analyses and deserve emphasis because they are where "one egg a day is fine" stops being universally true:

**(a) A geographic split.** The protective/neutral pattern is strongest in **Asian** cohorts (Drouin-Chartier's Asian subgroup **RR 0.92, 0.85–0.99**; verified above) and absent or slightly adverse in US/European cohorts. Both the *BMJ* authors and reviewers attribute this to confounding by overall dietary pattern, not a true biological difference — the same egg tracks a healthier diet in one setting and a less healthy one in another.

**(b) A heart-failure threshold.** Unlike CHD and stroke, **heart failure** shows a J-shaped signal: at ~1 egg/day, summary RR **1.15 (1.02–1.30)**, rising to **1.23 (1.06–1.44)** at ~9 eggs/week (Godos 2021; corroborated by an umbrella review pooling RR **1.25, 1.12–1.39** for ≥1 egg/day — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10200385/). This is a more consistent harm signal than the CHD data and argues against *high* intakes.

An overarching caveat: a 2025 umbrella review graded the overall certainty of this body of evidence as low, precisely because it rests on observational data with confounding and single-timepoint diet measurement. The honest summary is "reassuring but not high-certainty."

---

## 4. What the randomized trials actually show (the strongest design)

Cohorts can mislead through confounding; randomized controlled trials cannot in the same way. On the intermediate outcome that matters most — LDL cholesterol — the RCT evidence is clarifying:

- **Isolated dietary cholesterol does raise LDL, but modestly.** Meta-analyses of egg-feeding trials: adding eggs raised LDL-C by about **+8.1 mg/dL** (17 RCTs; 95% CI 4.5–11.8) but also nudged HDL up, leaving the LDL/HDL ratio only slightly worse (+0.14). — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7400894/ · The classic metabolic-ward work (Clarke, *BMJ* 1997) implies roughly **+1.9 to +4.6 mg/dL LDL per 100 mg** of added dietary cholesterol (about one egg), with the effect flattening at higher intakes. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2125600/ · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30596814/

- **In the context of a whole diet, eggs move cholesterol very little.** Feeding 3 eggs/day for 4 weeks to people with metabolic syndrome changed LDL by a non-significant +2.4%. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7257773/ · A 2025 crossover trial found LDL tracked **saturated fat, not egg cholesterol** — a low-saturated-fat diet *including* 2 eggs/day actually lowered LDL. — https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(25)00253-9/abstract

- **Even in people with type 2 diabetes, eggs did no harm in trials.** The **DIABEGG** RCTs (140 then 128 people with prediabetes/T2D) compared ~12 eggs/week vs <2/week for 3–12 months and found **no adverse difference** in LDL, HDL, triglycerides, HbA1c, weight, inflammation, or oxidative stress. — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25833969/ · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29741558/

The RCT takeaway is the crux of the whole question: **the cholesterol you eat has a much smaller effect on blood cholesterol than the saturated and trans fat you eat.** An egg boiled or poached behaves very differently, metabolically, from an egg fried in butter next to sausage.

---

## 5. Mechanisms — why the effect is smaller than "cholesterol → cholesterol" intuition suggests

- **The body compensates.** Dietary cholesterol suppresses the body's own cholesterol synthesis, and absorption efficiency varies widely (roughly 20–90% between individuals). This blunting is why one egg does not raise LDL by anything like the amount it contains.
- **"Hyper-responders" vs "hypo-responders."** Roughly **one-third of people** raise both LDL *and* HDL in response to dietary cholesterol (leaving the ratio largely preserved), while about two-thirds barely respond. In responders, the extra LDL tends to be the **larger, more buoyant (less atherogenic)** particle type rather than small, dense LDL. — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12672915/ · https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6126094/
- **The TMAO pathway is weak for whole eggs.** Choline in eggs can be converted by gut bacteria to TMAO, a molecule linked to atherosclerosis — but a 28-day RCT found **4 whole eggs/day did not significantly raise fasting TMAO** (2.0→2.3 µmol/L, NS), whereas a *free-choline supplement* raised it nearly 6-fold. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8410632/ (post-meal TMAO does rise with yolk load in some work — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4135488/ — so this pathway is real but modest for normal intakes.)
- **Eggs also carry genuinely good things:** high-quality protein, choline, and the carotenoids lutein and zeaxanthin (~330 µg/egg). This is part of why replacing eggs with refined carbs is *not* an improvement.

---

## 6. The one population that should be more cautious: people with diabetes

This is the most robust "harm" signal in the entire literature, and it recurs across independent analyses:

- CHD in people with diabetes, highest vs lowest egg intake: **RR 1.54 (1.14–2.09)** (Rong 2013).
- CVD in people with diabetes: **HR 1.69 (1.09–2.62)** (Shin 2013) and **RR 1.83 (1.42–2.37)** (Li 2013, *Atherosclerosis* — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23643053/).
- CVD in diabetics at ~1 egg/day: **SRR 1.22 (1.08–1.39)** (Godos 2021).
- Physicians' Health Study: high egg intake carried an all-cause mortality **HR 2.01 (1.26–3.20)** among diabetic men vs 1.22 in non-diabetics. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2386667/

Two honest counterweights keep this from being a flat prohibition: (1) In the *best-adjusted* cohorts (BMJ 2020), the diabetic point estimate shrank to a non-significant **HR 1.06 (0.81–1.39)** even though the statistical interaction remained — suggesting much of the excess is confounding, not causation. (2) The DIABEGG **randomized trials found no harm** from 12 eggs/week in people with diabetes (§4). The reasonable reading: the evidence for people with diabetes is genuinely mixed and leans toward *modest caution*, not avoidance.

There is a related **US-vs-elsewhere signal for developing type 2 diabetes**: per 1 egg/day, risk rose ~14–18% in US cohorts but was null-to-inverse in Europe and Asia (P-interaction ≈ 0.01), and the US association appeared **only in people with lower overall diet quality**. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7458776/ That last detail is the whole story in miniature: the eggs that "hurt" are the ones sitting next to processed meat and refined starch.

---

## 7. What the official guidelines say

- **American Heart Association (2019/2020 Science Advisory):** dropped a fixed cholesterol cap and concluded observational evidence "generally does not indicate a significant association" of dietary cholesterol with CVD; guidance should focus on overall dietary pattern. In plain-language terms the AHA states **healthy people can include up to a whole egg (or equivalent) per day**, and **older adults with normal cholesterol up to two**, while those with high LDL should cut both saturated fat and dietary cholesterol. — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31838890/ · https://www.heart.org/en/news/2023/08/25/heres-the-latest-on-dietary-cholesterol-and-how-it-fits-in-with-a-healthy-diet
- **Dietary Guidelines for Americans:** the 2015–2020 edition **removed the 300 mg/day cholesterol cap**; the 2020–2025 edition advises keeping dietary cholesterol "as low as practicable" within a healthy pattern rather than naming a number. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10285014/
- **British Heart Foundation:** **no set limit**; "1 or 2 eggs per day is unlikely to be a problem" as part of a balanced diet, with caution for familial hypercholesterolaemia. — https://www.bhf.org.uk/informationsupport/heart-matters-magazine/nutrition/are-eggs-high-in-cholesterol
- **European Society of Cardiology / EAS (2019 dyslipidaemia guideline):** the notable holdout — still recommends dietary cholesterol **<300 mg/day**, "particularly in people with high plasma cholesterol," and places eggs in the "in moderation" category. One large egg is ~185–200 mg, so this implicitly lands near ~1 egg/day for healthy people and lower for high-cholesterol patients. — https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/41/1/111/5556353
- **American Diabetes Association (2019 nutrition consensus):** sets **no specific egg limit** and notes the evidence does not support a strict dietary-cholesterol cap for the general population, while acknowledging the picture is "less clear" in diabetes.

---

## 8. Where the evidence genuinely disagrees, and how to weigh it

| Question | Best answer | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Does ~1 egg/day raise CHD/stroke risk in healthy adults? | No detectable effect | Moderate (consistent across the largest cohorts, meta-analyses, and RCTs on LDL) |
| Is there *any* credible harm signal? | Yes — one US pooled cohort (JAMA 2019), heart failure at higher intakes, and diabetes | Low–moderate; the JAMA signal is confounded by total dietary cholesterol |
| Do eggs *protect* the heart? | Probably not — the "benefit" is likely confounding in Asian diets | Low |
| Are eggs riskier for people with diabetes? | Plausibly yes, modestly | Mixed — strong in older cohorts, near-null in best-adjusted data, no harm in RCTs |
| What matters more than the egg? | Saturated fat and overall diet quality | High (RCT-supported) |

The reason "no effect" wins over "harm" for healthy people is a hierarchy-of-evidence judgment: the null is supported by the **largest, best-adjusted cohorts, the biggest meta-analysis, and — decisively — randomized trials** showing eggs barely move LDL in a whole-diet context. The harm signal rests on a single observational pooled analysis whose effect is entangled with total dietary cholesterol and measured diet only once. That said, the heart-failure threshold and the diabetes signal are consistent enough that the safe zone is "about one a day," not "unlimited."

---

## 9. Actionable recommendation

**For a healthy adult with normal cholesterol: about one egg a day is fine.** You do not need to fear it, count it anxiously, or default to egg-white omelets. Up to one whole egg daily is explicitly endorsed by the AHA and BHF and is not associated with heart disease in the strongest evidence. An occasional higher-egg day (a 3-egg brunch) is not a problem.

Refine that based on your situation:

- **If you have type 2 diabetes, established heart disease, familial hypercholesterolaemia, or an LDL your doctor is treating:** be more moderate — a common clinical convention is to keep whole eggs to roughly **3–4 per week** and prioritize cutting saturated fat. (Note: this specific weekly number is clinical practice, not a hard figure in the primary guidelines, which instead say "reduce saturated fat and dietary cholesterol together.") Randomized trials suggest even here the egg itself is not clearly harmful, so this is caution, not prohibition — discuss it with your clinician.

- **Watch the company the egg keeps, not just the egg.** The saturated fat in the butter, bacon, sausage, cheese, and the refined toast/hash-browns beside it does more to your LDL than the yolk does. An egg poached or boiled and eaten with vegetables, whole grains, or on wholegrain toast is a genuinely healthy meal; the same egg fried in butter next to processed meat is the version the worrying studies were really capturing.

- **Don't fix the egg by eating something worse.** Replacing eggs with sugary cereal or pastries is a downgrade. Where substitution helps, the data favor swapping toward yogurt, nuts, legumes, fish, or whole grains.

- **Keep high intakes occasional.** The one intake-related harm signal that recurs (heart failure) appears above ~1 egg/day sustained. Habitual 3-or-more-eggs-every-day is where the reassurance thins.

In one sentence: **an egg a day is a safe, nutritious habit for most healthy adults — spend your dietary vigilance on saturated fat and overall diet quality, and step down to a few eggs a week if you have diabetes or established heart disease.**
